newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel bonds close higher on CPI expectations.
newsitem.headline: Israel bonds close higher on CPI expectations.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher across the board on Wednesday with high demand for short and medium-term CPI-linked bonds on expectations of a high consumer price index (CPI), traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: +0.16 pct to 106.61
* CPI-linked government bonds: +0.17 pct to 106.84
* Unlinked government bonds: +0.13 pct to 106.29
* Dollar-linked government bonds: +0.15 pct to 105.39
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.06 to 105.16
Volume including Makams was 140 million shekels.
"There was demand and price rises across the board, with higher rises in CPI-linked bonds," said Dany Shamir of Israel Discount Bank.

"The market apparently is expecting an unpleasant surprise from the CPI. It is expecting a minimum CPI of 1.1 percent or even more. There was a chase for short-term and medium-term CPI-linked bonds but it is difficult to find supply of these," he said. "Prices of these bonds rose and their yields fell."
The April CPI, which is seasonally high due to the Passover holiday, will be published on Thursday after the close of the trading day.
"Yields of short-term and medium-term CPI-linked bonds are at around four percent," said Dany Alt at Nesuah Trading and Investment.

Prices were up in the unlinked sector as well. "There wasn't any trading for a few days, so prices have risen," said Shamir. The markets were closed on Sunday and Monday because of Memorial and Independence Days celebrations.
Alt said demand for bonds was high because of the tight supply. "Bank of Israel did not issue any new bonds this week (on behalf of the government)," he said. "All in all the market was positive."
Prices of dollar-linked bonds were up as well because of a strengthening of the dollar worldwide, Alt said.
He added that the market had little hopes for an immediate cut in interest rates. "We don't expect a change in the near future. Maybe in the summer months, when the CPIs will be lower," he said.
Israel's base rate is 13.9 percent, where it has been since the end of February. The Bank of Israel will announce any change at the end of May.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.40 shekels)
- Shoshanna Solomon, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211
